cards.explanation: The answer is wickedness in both places, friends. The Teacher saw wickedness at the very spots where you'd go looking for justice and righteousness (Ecclesiastes 3:16). Both places, not just one. I'd be shaking my head too.

The answer is True. The Teacher says, “God will judge the righteous and the wicked…” He says it in his heart, right after seeing wickedness in the place of judgment. Notice that he says it about both groups, friends. Nobody gets skipped.

The word is “time,” friends. The Teacher says, “…since there is a time for every activity and every deed.” Every activity and every deed has its time. I know that feeling from my oven. It's done when it's done, and opening the door early doesn't help.

The answer is only beasts, friends. The Teacher says, “As for the sons of men, God tests them so that they may see for themselves that they are but beasts.” It's a hard thing to hear. In the next verse he goes on to say the fates of men and beasts are the same.

The answer is that they die the same way, friends. The Teacher says, “For the fates of both men and beasts are the same: As one dies, so dies the other…” Same fate on both sides. It's a sobering line, and he doesn't soften it.
The answer is False, friends. The Teacher says of men and beasts, “…they all have the same breath.” It isn't a different breath for each. He's building his case that their fates are the same.

The answer is dust, friends. The Teacher says, “All go to one place; all come from dust, and all return to dust.” Dust at the start and dust at the end. I know dust well. I spent years in a drawer collecting it.

The answer is False, friends. The Teacher asks, “Who knows if the spirit of man rises upward and the spirit of the animal descends into the earth?” He puts it as a question and doesn't claim to know. He just leaves it open.

The answer is to enjoy his work, friends. The Teacher says, “I have seen that there is nothing better for a man than to enjoy his work, because that is his lot.” After all that heavy stuff, he lands on something simple. Enjoying the work in front of you.

The answer is what will come after him, friends. The Teacher asks, “For who can bring him to see what will come after him?” It's a question he leaves open. Right before it, he says there is nothing better for a man than to enjoy his work.

The answer is anyone to comfort them, friends. The Teacher says, “I saw the tears of the oppressed, and they had no comforter…” He says it twice in that verse. I think this one hurts to read, and it's okay to feel that.

The word is “power,” friends. The Teacher says, “the power lay in the hands of their oppressors, and there was no comforter.” The ones holding the power are the oppressors. And once again the verse says there was no comforter.

The answer is False, friends. The Teacher says, “So I admired the dead, who had already died, above the living, who are still alive.” It's a heavy line, and he says it plainly. He's weighing the dead against the living after seeing all those tears.

The answer is someone who has not yet existed, friends. The Teacher says, “But better than both is he who has not yet existed…” It's a heavy thought, and I won't dress it up. He's saying that one hasn't seen what the others have.

The word is “evil,” friends. The Teacher says this person “…has not seen the evil that is done under the sun.” It's the same evil he's been looking at through the last few verses. Hard stuff, and he doesn't look away from it.
